channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: How Bespoke faked AI until it actually worked (w/ Akemi Tsunagawa) | E2320
gist: Bespoke founder Akemi Tsunagawa walks Jason Calacanis through three businesses built off one thesis — Japan is structurally short of workers — from a 2015 multilingual chatbot she manually faked as a human, to smart-glasses vocational training for imported Vietnamese/Indonesian/Filipino labor, to scaffold- and paint-inspection robots for shipyards. The financing angle is the sleeper: ~450M yen raised, last round March 2020, then profitability funded by 10-year bank loans at ~1% collateralized by government contracts, plus a plan to roll up profitable-but-successor-less Japanese factories and shipyards.

themes.theme: Faking the bot: Bespoke's 2015 chatbot origin

insights.claim: Bespoke launched its multilingual tourist chatbot in 2015 by having humans, including founder Akemi Tsunagawa herself, pose as the bot on live conversations to prove demand before the technology worked.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Wizard-of-Oz manual delivery remains the cheapest way to validate an AI product before the model exists; treat 'faked' early AI demos as a signal of demand discipline, not fraud.
insights.quote: We also had human including myself chat with people uh pretending to be a bot.

insights.claim: Investors rejected Bespoke's 2015 chatbot on both technical and cultural grounds because no consumer chatbot was in active use at the time and AI was unpopular in Japan.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: A reminder that consensus VC pattern-matching prices timing, not insight; category-creating AI companies founded pre-2020 were funded on founder conviction rather than market comps.
insights.quote: The thing investors did not believe in was like how people would communicate with AI when they need help because back in 2015 AI was not popular at all.

insights.claim: Narita Airport signed Bespoke in 2017 not to chase AI but because information-counter staff kept quitting after being yelled at in Russian, Korean and Chinese — labor attrition, not technology appetite, drove the enterprise deal.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: The durable enterprise wedge for AI in Japan is staff attrition and unfillable roles, so sell against turnover cost rather than automation ROI.
insights.quote: our people keep quitting the job because it's stressful being like yelled at, uh, in Russian, Korean, Chinese, all sorts of different languages.

insights.claim: When Bespoke's chatbot broke during a Christmas peak and the founder personally answered users for a week, they discovered human-like small talk raised engagement, so they copied her transcripts into the bot and engagement rose sharply.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Deliberately making an assistant less efficient and more conversational can lift engagement — a design lever worth testing in any consumer-facing AI product.
insights.quote: during that time we learned that like humanlike communication actually uh increases the user engagement

insights.claim: Bespoke runs opposite chatbot designs by use case: tourism bots add chit-chat to raise engagement while its emergency-response bot strips conversation to deliver the evacuation center address immediately.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Conversational-AI vendors that ship one personality across use cases are mispositioned; the engagement-vs-speed tradeoff should be a product configuration, not a company-wide choice.
insights.quote: for emergency response you want the evacuation center address as soon as possible. So you don't want any chat chat but a different chatbot for different use case.

insights.claim: Japan now receives roughly 60 million tourists a year, and Akemi Tsunagawa attributes the largest share of that surge to the weak yen turning Japan from an expensive destination into one of the most affordable high-quality ones.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Japanese inbound-tourism revenue is levered to FX; a materially stronger yen would compress the volume tailwind under hotel, retail and travel names.
insights.quote: Japan used to be an expensive destination a long long time ago, right? But now I think it's one of the cheapest like the most affordable uh destination, you still get high quality.

insights.claim: The original trigger for Japan's tourism boom was a government decision to loosen visa requirements for non-Western tourists, who now make up the majority of arrivals — a policy change, not marketing.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Inbound volume is a policy-set variable; watch visa rule changes as the leading indicator for Japanese travel and retail demand, ahead of FX.
insights.quote: one of the uh trigger um before Japan became popular was the government's decision to um loosen the visa requirement for um non-western tourists to come in

insights.claim: Over-tourism has been a problem in Japan since roughly 2017-2018, with some restaurants and ryokan refusing non-Japanese guests entirely while the majority of shops and hotels now derive a major part of their profit from foreign visitors.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: The tourism trade in Japan is bifurcating between businesses monetizing foreigners and those excluding them — relevant to local hospitality asset selection and to regulatory risk of tourism caps.
insights.quote: over tourism has been a problem not just recently. It's been a problem probably even about like since 2017 2018 uh when we saw like the surge of tourists.

themes.theme: Depopulation and the imported blue-collar workforce

insights.claim: Japan currently loses roughly 700,000 to 800,000 people a year — the equivalent of Yamanashi Prefecture — and Akemi Tsunagawa expects that annual loss to accelerate toward 1 million.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: A shrinking base of ~1M people a year sets a hard ceiling on domestic demand and a hard floor under labor-substitution businesses: automation, immigration services and asset rollups.
insights.quote: every year we lose population equivalent of Yamanashi Prefecture that is around uh 700,000 to 800,000 and then this number would go up rapidly uh to 1 million

insights.claim: Japan's birth rate problem is fundamentally an affordability problem: having a family has become a luxury in Tokyo because wages have not kept up with inflation, and existing tax benefits are not enough to change the calculus.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Pro-natal fiscal tinkering will not reverse Japanese demographics without real wage growth, so the imported-labor and automation theses stay intact for a decade-plus.
insights.quote: So having family has become a luxury

insights.claim: Japan's government wage-increase pressure campaign only works at large companies, because smaller firms cannot pass price increases through to customers fast enough to fund higher pay.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Expect Japanese wage growth to stay concentrated in large caps and widen the large-vs-small firm margin gap — a screen for both SME distress and rollup opportunity.
insights.quote: not every company can transfer the price right so they can't just suddenly raise the service price to actually be able to increase pay uh for their workers.

insights.claim: Japan changed its regulations in 2019 after industry associations lobbied government, so non-Japanese blue-collar workers in listed industries can now enter as workers rather than trainees but are capped at five years unless they pass certain exams.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: The five-year cap plus exam gate creates a recurring, compulsory training and certification market — exactly the wedge Bespoke's Be Trained product sells into.
insights.quote: you are allowed to come in as the worker but you can only stay for five years unless you pass like certain exams then suddenly you can stay almost like permanently.

insights.claim: New Japanese rules are expected to require N4-level Japanese — roughly the fluency of a ten-year-old — for incoming foreign workers, raising the language bar on an already-constrained labor supply.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: A language gate shrinks the eligible labor pool while boosting demand for Japanese-language training providers; she flags uncertainty on the exact requirement.
insights.quote: I think it was almost like you need to be speaking Japanese like a 10 years old.

insights.claim: The Japanese labor shortage is already destroying industrial capacity: shipbuilders with orders booked three years out have cut annual output from about nine ships to six purely because they cannot staff the work.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Japanese industrial capacity is supply-constrained by headcount rather than demand, so revenue upside sits with whoever restores throughput — automation vendors and acquirers of under-utilized yards.
insights.quote: these ship building companies have orders booked for the next three years.

insights.claim: Bespoke's Be Trained product has Japanese trade specialists wear smart glasses to record and narrate their work, then converts the footage into multi-language training videos with auto-generated quizzes so HR managers can verify comprehension.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Capturing tacit trade knowledge from retiring specialists via wearables is a repeatable model wherever an aging skilled workforce meets non-native labor — including the Gulf states.
insights.quote: what we do is we send out smart glasses and then have the wallpaper specializ specialists like put on the glasses and record how they do things.

insights.claim: Bespoke's move into robotics was pulled by customers: a year or two into the training product, shipbuilders and construction firms told them there was a ceiling on what non-Japanese workers could be trained to do and asked what else could be automated.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Immigration is a partial fix at best; the same customers buying labor-import services become the buyers of automation, making training-to-robotics a natural expansion path.
insights.quote: there's only so much we can do with non-Japanese workers.

insights.claim: Japanese law requires manual daily inspection of scaffolds before use, but no company has the resources to do it and firms skip it close to 100% of the time, producing injuries and fatalities.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: A universally-ignored legal mandate is a latent compliance market: robotic inspection converts an unenforced rule into a budget line the moment liability or enforcement tightens.
insights.quote: They skip it almost 100% of the time.

insights.claim: Bespoke's inspection robot autonomously climbs scaffolds, grabs and shakes each joint, records whether it is safe, and routes the inspection record to the person accountable for repairs — with shiny-metal reflections at shipyards and plants the hardest technical obstacle.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Physical actuation plus vision on reflective industrial surfaces is the real moat here, not the AI; incremental inspections are near-zero marginal cost once the robot is deployed.
insights.quote: graphs the joint, shakes it and then record each joint is safe or not and then send the inspection records to uh whoever is actually in charge of the inspection.

insights.claim: Because scaffold inspection generates no profit and is a hard sell, Bespoke bundled higher-value inspections onto the same robot — notably paint-thickness inspection, where companies building ships over 200 meters spend more than a thousand human hours per vessel.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: The commercial unlock for industrial robots is finding the measurable-hours task adjacent to the safety task; one robot amortized across three or four inspection types changes the payback math.
insights.quote: some companies that produce ship over like 200 mters they would be spending uh more than thousand human hours to do the paint thickness inspection.

insights.claim: Bespoke raised roughly 450 million yen (about $3 million) in equity, took its last round in March 2020 at the onset of COVID, and has been self-sufficient ever since across three business lines.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: A three-product Japanese company built on ~$3M of equity is a capital-efficiency benchmark that reframes what Japanese startups actually need from VCs.
insights.quote: the but the last round was back in 2020. So March 2020 like right in the middle of COVID and then we've been self-sufficient ever since.

insights.claim: Bespoke funds growth with Japanese bank loans collateralized by its government contracts — the loan equals the collateral amount, short-term loans run until the contract is paid, long-term loans stretch to 10 years at roughly 1% interest, and the process is faster than raising from investors.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: For govtech and public-sector startups in Japan, contract-collateralized 1% debt is a materially cheaper capital stack than equity — a structural advantage US-based comparables cannot replicate.
insights.quote: I learned along the way that like we can use the bank uh government contract as the collaterals

insights.claim: Japanese banks will lend readily to a startup once it is profitable, whereas in the US, per Jason Calacanis, banks lend against existing assets so early founders are limited to American Express and Visa credit lines repayable in 30 to 60 days.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Profitability in Japan unlocks cheap leverage and lets founders retain equity — an argument for underwriting Japanese startups on cash generation rather than growth-at-all-costs.
insights.quote: so it's a bit difficult for startups but as soon as we turn profitable it was quite easy

themes.theme: Successor-less factories and rural asset arbitrage

insights.claim: Many Japanese companies that go bankrupt are actually profitable and fail only because the owners have no successor or children to take over, while younger generations do not want to be factory owners.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: A pipeline of profitable Japanese SMEs available at distressed prices, possibly below one times revenue and potentially with owner financing — the setup for a search-fund or rollup strategy.
insights.quote: there are u many companies that go bankrupt here are actually profitable. They simply don't have successors.

insights.claim: Bespoke's stated plan is to buy a small shipyard or factory, deploy its own robots there to demonstrate efficiency, kaizen the operation, and only then export the model overseas — treating asset ownership as go-to-market rather than pure M&A.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: Owning the customer site to prove automation ROI is a capital-intensive but credible answer to slow industrial sales cycles; Calacanis explicitly urged her to raise for a factory rollup.
insights.quote: so we'll buy, let's say, like a small shipyard and then deploy our own robots to show them how efficient it could be.

insights.claim: Despite the same labor and integration problems existing in UAE, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, Bespoke is staying domestic because Japan is the hottest market for at least the next two years.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: The Gulf is the identified second market for labor-training and inspection automation; expect expansion only after the robot-plus-owned-factory model is proven in Japan.
insights.quote: right now we think at least for the next two years or so Japan is the hottest market.

insights.claim: Rural Japanese towns are hollowing out through a specific mechanism: there is often no local high school, so children leave at high-school or university age and never return because there are no jobs, leaving countryside houses collapsing and available for free or near-free.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Cheap rural Japanese property plus ski-season rental demand is an active arbitrage — Calacanis cites Americans renovating Hokkaido houses and one who took over an abandoned ski resort from the local town.
insights.quote: Once they leave, they don't come back because there's no job.

themes.theme: AI headcount substitution and the Slack oracle

insights.claim: Bespoke runs 65 people with more than half non-Japanese, and when its Germany-based engineer moved home last year the company chose not to backfill the role because AI coding agents had made code review fast enough to absorb the work.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa
insights.so_what: A concrete non-backfill decision at a 65-person company is the clearest observable form of AI headcount substitution — watch for the same pattern in portfolio hiring plans.
insights.quote: last year when our German um Germany engineer had to move back to her country we didn't replace her

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says his firm now asks portfolio startups to explain, at every new hire decision, whether the role should be a human or automated with AI — with the inflection appearing around 60 people where firms would historically add three accountants, three HR staff and three assistants.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Back-office headcount at the 60-person scaling point is the first line item AI removes; model portfolio company burn with flatter G&A curves than historical comps.

insights.claim: AI-written job descriptions now outperform ones Calacanis previously paid $1,000 to $2,000 per document for, because the models have indexed every job board in every language — a capability no individual human could ever have had.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Corpus coverage, not reasoning, is why AI beats experts on template-shaped work — a useful test for which professional services categories get commoditized next.
insights.quote: There's never been a human who had all the job descriptions in the world in their brain.

insights.claim: Calacanis is building a 'second CEO' by connecting Claude Cowork to Slack Enterprise Plus, Gmail, Notion and calendar so it can read every message and DM, replace the weekly human status report, and eventually advise on what the CEO should do next.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Slack Enterprise Plus becomes the required tier for full-history AI access — a concrete upsell driver for collaboration vendors as companies build internal oracles.
insights.quote: So I have been thinking about creating a second CEO like uh but that CEO has access to every email of every person in the company at all times

insights.claim: Akemi Tsunagawa has deliberately not connected an AI oracle to Bespoke's internal messages on privacy grounds, while Calacanis argues disclosure solves it — and separately raises recreating departed employees as AI personas, an idea both agree needs name-and-likeness permission or a renamed persona.
insights.speaker: Akemi Tsunagawa and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Consent and likeness rights are the real adoption brake on company-wide AI oracles and synthetic ex-employees — a compliance product gap and a legal risk for vendors shipping these features.
insights.quote: part of me feels like we shouldn't be going through some of the messages even though I am not going to personally go through them.
